opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that stands out most about Abhinav is how much they think from first principles. A lot of people, when they hit a problem, reach for whatever the field currently treats as the standard approach. Abhinav tends to step back and ask: what are we actually trying to do here, and why do we believe the current approach is the right one?

They're also very comfortable holding an idea that sounds a bit crazy for a while before judging it. In conversations they'll say, "Okay, suppose this were true, what would the world have to look like?" Then they follow that chain of reasoning quite far. Sometimes it goes nowhere, but sometimes it leads somewhere really interesting that nobody else was looking at, because everyone else dismissed the starting point too early.

And there's a strong empirical streak too. It's not only abstract reasoning. Once an idea seems promising, they want to find the smallest, cleanest experiment that could prove it wrong. I find that combination pretty rare: bold in the hypotheses, but very disciplined about testing them.

The last thing I'd mention is taste. They have a good sense of which problems are worth spending years on and which are just incremental. Talking with them often reframes what you think the important question is, and for me that's been one of the most valuable parts of working together.

r001.rationale: The response says Abhinav’s unusual ideas can lead somewhere interesting and may be dismissed too early, but it does not say their interest becomes apparent only after an initial period of not understanding them.

fable-5.1.text:
Abhinav's way of thinking is, I'd say, almost aggressively first-principles. He doesn't start from what the field is doing. He starts from a question like, "What is the actual problem here, and why is it hard?" And he'll sit in that discomfort much longer than most people are willing to.

One thing I noticed working with him is that he's deeply skeptical of benchmarks as a proxy for progress. Most of us, when we're junior, want to find a leaderboard and climb it, because that's legible. He'd push back on that constantly. He'd ask, "If you get three more points on this number, has the robot actually learned anything it couldn't do before?" And often the honest answer was no. That was uncomfortable, but it reshaped how I evaluate my own work.

The second thing is that he thinks in terms of data and scale before it was fashionable in robotics. He had this conviction, years ago, that the bottleneck wasn't the algorithm, it was the lack of diverse real-world experience, and that you have to build the infrastructure to collect it, even if it's unglamorous. He was willing to spend a lot of effort on things that didn't produce a paper right away, because he believed the compounding payoff would come later. And I think he's been proven mostly right.

And then there's a kind of contrarian instinct. If everyone agrees something is the right direction, his first reaction is to ask what's being overlooked. Not for the sake of being different, but because he genuinely believes the interesting problems live in the places the consensus has stopped looking. Sometimes that leads to dead ends. But when it works, it works in a way that incremental research never does.

What I try to carry forward from him is mostly the habit of asking "why" one more time than feels comfortable. He made it very hard to hide behind a result.

r001.rationale: The response describes Abhinav’s challenging questions and contrarian thinking, but does not say his ideas become interesting or compelling only after an initial period of not understanding them.
